nodes.text: When we arrived where she was lodging, we went in and found her tossing restlessly on her bed, her eyes drenched with love. When she had embraced her father in the usual way and he asked what was wrong, she said a headache was troubling her and she would gladly rest if she were allowed. Alarmed at this, Charicles slipped out of the room with me, ordering the maids to keep quiet, and when he had come out in front of the house he said, “What is this, my good Calasiris? What is this sickness that has come upon my little daughter?” “Do not be surprised,” I said, “if, after parading in procession before so many people, she has drawn some evil eye upon herself.” He gave an ironic laugh and said, “What, do you too, like the common crowd, believe there is such a thing as the evil eye?” “As much as anything else that is true,” I said. “It works like this. This air that surrounds us, passing deep inside through the eyes and the nostrils and the breath and the other passages, and carrying in with it the qualities from outside, sows in those who receive it an affection of the same kind as itself as it flows in; so that whenever someone looks on what is beautiful with envy, he fills the surrounding air with a hostile quality and blows his own breath, full of bitterness, onto the person near him. And this, being made of fine particles, penetrates right into the very bones and marrow; and envy has become a sickness for many, taking on its own name, the evil eye. Consider this too, Charicles: how many people have been infected with eye disease, how many with the conditions that come from plagues, without ever touching the sick, nor sharing the same bed or the same table, but only sharing the same air. Let the birth of love, too, prove the argument to you, if anything does: love, whose beginning is given by things seen, and whose passions are shot into souls through the eyes as if carried on the wind. And with good reason: for of the passages and senses in us, sight, being the most mobile and the hottest, is the most receptive to emanations, and with the fiery spirit that belongs to it, the passing-over of love

Day had not yet properly begun to break when there was a knocking at the inner door, and I heard someone calling the servant boy. When the servant asked who was knocking at the door, or on what business, the caller said, “Announce that it is Theagenes the Thessalian.” I was glad when the young man was announced to me, and told them to call him in, thinking that chance itself was giving me a starting point for the plans I had in hand. For I guessed that, having heard at the banquet that I was an Egyptian and a prophet, he had come to take me on as a helper in his love, suffering, I suppose, from the error of the many, who are deceived into thinking that the wisdom of the Egyptians is one and the same, because they know it badly. For one kind is common and, as one might say, goes along the ground; it is the handmaid of phantoms and grovels about the bodies of the dead; it pores over herbs and relies on incantations; it neither comes itself to any good end nor brings those who use it to one, but mostly trips itself up, and now and then achieves some paltry and meagre successes: illusions of things that are not as though they were, and disappointments of what was hoped for; it is the inventor of unlawful deeds and the servant of licentious pleasures. The other, my son, the true wisdom, of which that first one is a bastard that has borrowed its name, which we priests and the prophetic caste practise from our youth, looks upward to the heavens; it keeps company with the gods and shares in the nature of the higher beings; it investigates the motion of the stars and gains foreknowledge of the future; it stands aloof from these earthly evils, and pursues all things toward what is noble and useful to men. It was because of this wisdom that I too left my homeland for a time, in case I might somehow, as I told you before, escape what it had foretold me, the war of my sons against each other. But let these matters be left to the gods, and to the Fates as well, who have the power to make things happen or not; who, it seems, laid on me my exile from my homeland not so much for these reasons as for the finding of Charicleia.

When she had said this, Calasiris explained everything to Charicleia and, taking her with him, moved away. After going a little way beyond the bodies lying there, they came upon a low mound. There he lay down, putting the quiver under his head, while Charicleia sat, using the bag as a seat. The moon was just rising and lighting up everything with a bright light (for it happened to be the third day after the full moon); and Calasiris, being an old man in any case and worn out by the journey, was overcome by sleep, but Charicleia, kept awake by the cares that beset her, became the spectator of a scene that was unholy, though customary among Egyptian women. For the old woman, thinking she had got a time free of disturbance and unobserved, first dug a pit, and then lit a pyre on one side of it. Laying out the body of her son between the two, she took up an earthenware bowl from a tripod standing nearby and poured honey into the pit, then milk from another, and from a third she poured a libation of wine. Then she took a cake made with suet, moulded in the likeness of a man, crowned it with laurel and fennel, and threw it into the pit. After all this she took up a sword and, whirling herself into a frenzy of possession, prayed at length to the moon with barbarous names strange to the ear; then she gashed her arm, wiped off some of the blood with a sprig of laurel, and sprinkled it on the pyre. And after performing other prodigies besides, she bent over her son's corpse and, chanting something into his ear, roused him and by her sorcery forced him to stand upright. Charicleia, who had not watched even the first part without fear, now shuddered, and terrified by these unaccustomed happenings she woke Calasiris and made him a spectator of what was being done. Being in the dark, they themselves were not seen, but they could more easily watch what went on in the light by the pyre, and since they were not far off they could hear what was said, for the old woman was now questioning the corpse in a louder voice. Her question was whether his brother, her surviving son, would come back home safe. He answered nothing, but only nodded, ambiguously letting his mother hope for what she wished; then he suddenly collapsed and lay face down. She turned the body over on its back and would not give up her questioning, but with more violent compulsions, as it seemed, chanting much into his ears again, and leaping sword in hand now to the pyre, now to the pit, she roused him once more, and when he stood up she questioned him on the same matters, forcing him to make the prophecy clear not by nods alone but by voice as well. While the old woman was so occupied, Charicleia earnestly begged Calasiris that they too should go near what was happening and ask something about Theagenes. But he refused, saying that even watching was unholy, though he put up with it because it was forced on them; for it was not fitting for a prophet either to undertake such acts or to be present at them; rather, for prophets the gift of divination came from lawful sacrifices and pure prayers, but for the profane, who truly grovel about the earth and the bodies of the dead, in the way the chance of the moment had allowed them to see the Egyptian woman doing.
